source.title: Active Budget Allocation for Efficient Scaling Law Estimation via Surrogate-Guided Pruning
source.authors: Viktoria Schram; Markus Hiller; Daniel Beck; Trevor Cohn

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how well power-law scaling fits and extrapolations can be estimated from partial learning curves, using comparisons with full-data or synthetic ground-truth fits. It does not reproduce the original scaling-law experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports many comparisons of budget-allocation methods by minimum loss (Tables 1–2 and appendices) and noisy-curve results (Figures 3–4). Those evaluate allocation performance, not whether the claim's scaling relations hold, so they are not included as rows. Results based on cited studies are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a method paper: it uses scaling-law fits as a tool to score budget-allocation methods (SH, SH LMC, GP extrapolation). Most of its results are its own method's performance, which is T4-like. It does report, in a new nanoGPT/FineWeb-edu setting, that the fitted loss-compute law changes with the set of models used: slope 0.058 for all 90 curves versus 0.065 for a selected, fully trained subset, and different laws for small- versus large-model sets (Appendix I). That bears on V7 only. It reports no fit quality, residuals or comparison with alternative forms for V1. It does not test extrapolation to larger real runs for V2, and its synthetic curves are generated from scaling laws, so they cannot test V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SH, especially with surrogates, yields learning curves giving scaling laws close to their reference fits at a fraction of the compute (up to 98.7% savings). They add that LMC/GP extrapolation improves fits beyond the budget and that UCB/LCB fits give uncertainty ranges. The extrapolation benefit is shown only on synthetic curves generated from a Kaplan-style law. The authors acknowledge that validation is limited to nanoGPT up to 1.5B parameters and leave larger-scale validation open.
record.recipe_differences: This is a resource-allocation and surrogate-extrapolation study, not a reproduction of Kaplan or Hoffmann training sweeps or their compute-optimal allocation procedure. It fits loss-compute frontiers from nanoGPT and synthetic curves; model allocation uses Successive Halving and LMC/Deep Ensemble surrogates.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling-law fit depends on model set and compute range. Results also vary with budget, SH versus SH LMC, and—in the synthetic extrapolation experiments—GP mean versus UCB/LCB. The paper additionally evaluates several synthetic noise types and intensities, but those results concern allocation performance rather than scaling-law validity.

fits_no_version.finding: Budget-allocation methods (SH, SH LMC, GP extrapolation) recover reference loss-compute fits with small AbC at 75–98.7% lower training cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law fits can be estimated accurately from strategically truncated learning curves at a fraction of full training cost.

record.code_released: Publicly available according to the paper; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Direct experiments cover a single nanoGPT family up to 1.5B parameters and a fixed 10B-token data split. The synthetic extrapolation test is built from scaling-law patterns and is not validation on independently trained larger models. The full-data and entire-learning-curve references are fitted estimates rather than an external gold standard. Some fitted-law coefficients are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1–2, Appendix Figures 3–4 and Appendices K–L report minimum-loss or allocation-method comparisons, not direct tests of the claim's scaling-law relations. Other detailed allocation metrics and synthetic-noise outcomes are omitted for the same reason.

untested.parts: No fit quality, no N- or D-scaling, and only about two decades of compute; the power-law form is assumed, not tested.
No prediction of actual larger runs; the synthetic extrapolation is circular.
Not tested. The frontier is data-constrained (10B tokens), explicitly not compute-optimal.
Layer count and width vary, but there is no fixed-N comparison.
Not tested; only mentioned as future work.
Parameter counting, training schedule, data, fitting method and bending away from a power law are not tested; only model-set dependence is shown.

record.verdict_notes: Borderline T4: the core contribution is a method, scored by AbC against fitted references. Only incidental model-set-dependence results bear on V7, so the V7 label is thin (one illustrated run, plus one figure without values). Record values lost exponents (104→10^4, 1018→10^18). Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits loss against compute on a compute-efficient frontier; it does not separately test loss scaling with parameter count or tokens while the other quantities are not bottlenecks, nor the claim across several orders of magnitude in general.

It compares partial-data fitted laws with full-data or fully trained references and evaluates surrogate extrapolation, but does not demonstrate that power laws fitted on small runs predict actual runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study does not estimate how loss-minimising parameter and token counts grow with compute or compare their growth rates.
Although nanoGPT models vary in layer count and embedding dimension, the study does not isolate architectural effects at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning regime, or transfer setting is tested.
The study does not measure downstream task performance; it mentions downstream metrics only as future work.

The study examines effects of model set, budget allocation, and surrogate choice on fitted loss-compute laws. It does not test parameter-counting choices, alternative training schedules or data regimes as causes of exponent changes, compute-optimal parameter/token splits, or systematic bending away from a power law.
